background.definition: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) arises when there is narrowing of the arteries distal to the arch of the aorta. Intermittent claudication is defined as muscle discomfort in the lower limbs and is produced by exercise and relieved within 10 minutes of rest. Critical limb ischemia is present when there is ischemic rest pain or ischemic skin lesions (ulcers or gangrene).

list.listitem: Intermittent claudication in men: 4.1 to 12.9/1000/year
Intermittent claudication in women: 3.3 to 8.2/1000/year

The prevalence of PAD in the lower limbs, based on an ankle-brachial pressure index of less than 0.9, ranges from 139 to 169 per 1000 in men older than 55 years and 114 to 205 per 1000 women older than 55 years.
The prevalence of PAD increases with age; up to 20% of men and women older than 70 years have PAD.
Atheroma/atherosclerosis
Thrombus formation
Embolization from heart or central arteries
Arteritis
External compression (cystic adventitial disease/popliteal entrapment)
Atherosclerosis is the most common cause of chronic PAD.
Atherosclerosis results in gradual stenosis and occlusion of peripheral arteries leading to different levels of peripheral ischemia.

Secondary prevention with antiplatelets, statins, smoking cessation, antihypertensives, exercise training, and effective diabetic control reduces cardiovascular events and mortality in patients with PAD. A
The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends against routine screening for PAD.B
Screening for PAD is possible using ankle-brachial pressure indices. This has been recommended by some experts, although is not widely practiced.
Detecting asymptomatic PAD would allow the identification of patients at risk of further cardiovascular events and early treatment of risk factors to reduce these risks.

However, there is no evidence at present to indicate that early identification of PAD will result in the reduction of risk factors or that the latter would improve outcomes in asymptomatic PAD patients. It is therefore not recommended by the USPSTF.

A large Danish trial randomized men age 65 to 74 years to intensive cardiovascular screening (that included screening for PAD using ankle brachial index) or usual care. After 5 years it found PAD in 11.5% but no difference in amputations (0.9% vs 1.0%) and an overall reduction in mortality only in the younger patients (65 to 69, NNT = 91).
Secondary prevention is aimed at reducing cardiovascular events.
Smoking cessation should be encouraged through physician advice, behavioral therapy, nicotine replacement treatment, and bupropion or varenicline.
All symptomatic PAD patients should have their low-density lipoprotein cholesterol lowered according to ACC/AHA guidelines for cardiovascular disease.
ACC guidelines (2017) state that a screening duplex ultrasound for abdominal aortic aneurysm is reasonable in patients with symptomatic PAD.
Blood pressure should be controlled to <140/90; if the patient has diabetes or renal insufficiency, the goal is <130/80.

Patients with diabetes and PAD should control their glucose levels to achieve Hb A1c levels as close to 7% as possible. Recent studies such as the ACCORD, VADT, and ADVANCE trial have found worse outcomes with lower blood sugar targets, especially among high-risk cardiovascular patients.
All PAD patients should be prescribed a long-term antiplatelet agent. However, the combination of warfarin plus aspirin is no more effective than aspirin alone.
Reproducible muscle discomfort on exercise that is relieved within 10 minutes of resting (claudication) is highly indicative of PAD. B
An ankle-brachial pressure index is the recommended initial office test; a result of less than 0.9 indicates the presence of PAD. B
Duplex ultrasonography is a useful and reliable noninvasive test for assessing PAD. B
Other diagnostic tests such as MRA, CT angiography, and digital subtraction angiography may be necessary to identify the anatomic location and degree of stenosis. B

Pain subsides slowly on resting; quicker relief on elevating limb

list.listitem: Intermittent claudication is the first symptom of PAD. This is characterized by muscle discomfort in the lower limbs that is reproducibly brought on by exercise and relieved within 10 minutes of resting.

Peripheral pulses (ie, femoral artery) may be reduced or absent in patients with PAD. Audible bruits, particularly over the course of the common femoral and superficial femoral artery, indicate the presence of a stenosis.
Cold or discolored peripheries, loss of hair, and ulceration all suggest PAD.
Patients should be examined for the presence of non-healing ulcers or wounds.
Critical limb ischemia should be suspected and evaluated in patients with rest pain, nonhealing wounds, or gangrene.

The absence of a femoral pulse or the presence of a femoral bruit make PAD highly likely. Similarly, in patients with intermittent claudication, pain on walking will subside within 10 minutes of walking.
If a patient does not have any pain in the calf on walking, particularly uphill, it is unlikely that the patient is suffering from intermittent claudication.

A resting ankle-brachial pressure index of less than 0.9 is an accurate, noninvasive, and simple test to perform at the bedside. An ABI value less than 0.90 is 57% to 79% sensitive and 83% to 99% specific for arterial stenosis of at least 50%. In some patients, however, the test cannot be performed because of arterial calcification or ulcers in the gaiter area. Toe-brachial pressure indices could be performed in such cases.

Arterial ultrasonography is very accurate in assessing the presence of disease in the iliofemoral and femoropopliteal segments. Although this test is very user dependent, it is noninvasive. Color-guided Doppler ultrasound may be more sensitive than standard duplex ultrasound.

American College of Cardiology (ACC) and European College of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines both recommend duplex ultrasound as the initial imaging method, especially when revascularization is being considered.
MRA and CT angiography is recommended for mapping the arterial tree and guiding decision making regarding revascularization by ACC guidelines (2017).

Digital subtraction angiography is the gold standard investigation for PAD but is invasive and requires catheterization of peripheral arteries. ACC guidelines (2017) recommend that it be considered for patients with lifestyle-limiting claudication for whom revascularization is being considered.

Patients with suspected critical limb ischemia should have toe-brachial index with waveforms, transcutaneous oxygen pressure, and skin perfusion pressure measured, and if abnormal have anatomic assessment beginning with duplex ultrasound and often including CT angiography or MRA.

A prospective cohort study in 305 patients with diabetes concluded that a point of care duplex ultrasound test ("PAD-scan") and visual monophasic Doppler were both accurate for diagnosis of peripheral arterial disease in this population.
Take a careful clinical history, with detailed enquiry about symptoms, and examine pulses. Easily palpable peripheral pulses make PAD extremely unlikely.
Measure ankle-brachial pressure index; a value of less than 0.9 indicates presence of PAD.
Patients with noncompressible arteries and ABI >1.40 should have a toe brachial index assessed.

In some cases when doubt persists about the cause of symptoms with near-normal ankle-brachial pressure index, an exercise test may be required (with measurement of ankle-brachial pressure before and after exercise). In the presence of significant stenoses, the ankle-brachial pressure index will drop significantly after exercise.
Duplex ultrasonography is first-line imaging. MR angiograph or CT angiography can indicate the site and severity of the arterial disease, especially if revascularization is being considered.

Regular exercise improves walking distance and maximal exercise time in patients with intermittent claudication. Only 50% of patients enrolled in a supervised walking program will require subsequent interventions in a recent clinical study.
Supervised exercise training appears to be more effective than home based walking programs or walking advice.A
Cilostazol improves symptoms in patients with intermittent claudication in the absence of heart failure. A

Consider endovascular revascularization for patients with intermittent claudication and inadequate response to exercise or pharmacological therapy A or critical ischemia. This may involve angioplasty with or without stenting.B
Open surgery (eg, endarterectomy or bypass surgery) is an option for revascularization, particularly in patients with critical limb ischemia. C

An antiplatelet agent (aspirin or clopidogrel) should be prescribed to patients with PAD; they reduce the risk of nonfatal stroke.A Ticagrelor is no more effective than clopidogrel (and less well tolerated) in reducing cardiovascular events. Adding rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily to aspirin decreases limb ischemia events (NNT =44) but increases bleeding events (NNH = 83).B

ACC guidelines (2017) recommend that an antiplatelet agent (either aspirin 75-325 mg/day or clopidogrel 75 mg/day) should be prescribed to patients with symptomatic PAD. Ticagrelor is no more effective and not as well tolerated as clopidogrel in PAD. Subjects with artificial grafts may benefit from antiplatelet agents.
The value of antiplatelet agents is less clear but is deemed "reasonable" by ACC guidelines (2017) in patients with asymptomatic PAD.

Anticoagulants are starting to play more of a role in PAD management. The combination of warfarin plus aspirin is no more effective than aspirin alone, but in subjects who undergo infrainguinal venous grafting to treat lower extremity PAD, warfarin may be more beneficial than antiplatelet agents for maintaining graft patency. The VOYAGER PAD trial found that adding rivaroxaban to aspirin after lower extremity revascularization is associated with decreased limb ischemia (NNT = 44) but at increased risk of bleeding (NNH = 83).
A secondary analysis of the VOYAGER PAD trial found that for patients over age 75 years, the NNT to decrease limb ischemia was 26 and the NNH was 123 for major bleeding.
The combination of rivaroxaban and aspirin reduces cardiovascular mortality in patients with chronic PAD.
ACC guidelines (2017) recommend cilostazol as an effective therapy for symptomatic patients with PAD. The guidelines also recommend against use of pentoxyfilline.

A Cochrane review of 16 RCTs with 3972 participants found a significantly greater initial claudication distance (26.5 meters) and absolute claudication distance (40 meters) compared with placebo. There was low quality evidence that quality of life was improved. Headache was reported more often by persons taking cilostazol (OR 2.8).

In studies comparing cilostazol with pentoxifylline, there was no significant difference in outcomes. There was no evidence that cilostazol impacted amputation rates or need for surgical intervention.

Thrombolytic therapy, including intraluminal thrombolysis, is an option for patients with critical limb ischemia if there is appropriate expertise available, although risk of bleeding complications is high. A systematic review found no evidence of a difference in outcomes for different infusion techniques, dosage regimens, or adjunctive agents.
A trial randomized 792 patients with T2DM and PAD to semaglutide or placebo. The gain in walking distance after 1 year was significantly greater in the semaglutide group (21% vs 8%).
A statin is recommended by ACC guidelines (2017) for all patients with PAD.
Nicotine replacement treatment, bupropion, and, more recently, varenicline have been found to increase smoking cessation rates in combination with other treatment modalities.

Antihypertensives are routinely recommended to achieve target blood pressure levels, although studies specifically in patients with PAD are lacking. ACC guidelines (2017) preferentially recommend ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers for treatment of hypertension in patients with PAD. In small studies, ramipril therapy is associated with an increase in pain free walking distance.
Naftidrofuryl has also been shown to improve walking distance in patients with claudication.
Omega-3 fatty acids do not influence pain-free walking distances, maximum walking distances, or the ankle-brachial pressure index.
A randomized trial with 202 participants found no benefit of metformin over placebo on walking distance.
A meta-analysis found 5 studies of prostaglandin E1 and concluded that this drug improves walking time in patients with intermittent claudication.
The impact of progenitor cell based therapy in PAD is unclear.

A meta-analysis identified 12 studies with 1423 patients randomized to propionyl-L-carnitine 1 to 2 grams daily or placebo, and found significant improvements in mean maximal walking distance (50 meters) and pain-free walking distance (33 meters). The drug was well tolerated.

ACC guidelines (2017) recommend that endovascular revascularization should be considered for patients with intermittent claudication who have had an inadequate response to exercise or pharmacological therapy or critical ischemia. This may involve angioplasty with or without stenting, although the benefit of stenting versus balloon angiography or drug-coated ballon angiography has not been definitively proven.

However, an individual patient data meta-analysis identified 8 studies with 2185 persons comparing paclitaxel-coated stents with balloon angioplasty for peripheral vascular disease. Mortality was higher after a median 4 years of follow-up (HR 1.38, 95% CI 1.06 - 1.80). The absolute mortality risk was 13.7% in the balloon angioplasty group and 18.3% in the paclitaxel stent group (absolute difference 4.6%, NNTH = 21).

One RCT showed that patients receiving paclitaxel-coated devices had no difference in incidence of death after 1 and 4 years compared with those who received an uncoated stent. Another RCT with 2355 patients found no impact of paclitaxel coating on amputation rates in patients with chronic limb-threatening iscehmia.

A Cochrane review of intravascular brachytherapy (use of radiation locally to prevent restenosis) identified 8 trials with a total of 1090 participants that compared usual care with PTA (with or without stenting) to usual care with PTA plus brachytherapy. The studies found some improvements in patency and reductions in restenosis, but no differences regarding cardiovascular events, mortality, quality of life, limb loss, or complications.

Infrainguinal venous grafting may be more successful with concomitant treatment with warfarin than with antiplatelet agents. By contrast, patients receiving artificial grafts my fare better with antiplatelet agents.

Open surgery (eg, endarterectomy or bypass surgery) is one of the options for revascularization, particularly in patients with critical limb ischemia. A systematic review found that autologous veins were preferred for above-the-knee femoral-popliteal bypass, with greater long-term patency.
In patients with chronic limb-threatening ischemia, outcomes are better for surgery than for endovascular procedures in the subgroup with a single greater saphenous vein segment suitable for bypass.

Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty improves claudication symptoms at 6 months. One systematic review found that percutaneous transluminal angioplasty was less effective in improving patency than open surgical bypass at 12 to 24 months.

The BASIL-3 trial randomized 481 patients with chronic limb-threatening ischemia to femoro-popliteal plain balloon angioplasty with or without bare metal stenting (PBA+/-BMS), drug coated balloon angioplasty with or without bare metal stenting (DCA+/-BMS), or drug eluting stenting. Major amputation or death occurred in 66% patients in the PBA+/-BMS group, 60% in the DCA+/-BMS group, and 58% in the drug eluting stent group. These differences were not statistically significant.
Phlebotomy to reduce iron stores did not improve mortality or other key clinical outcomes in a study of 1277 patients with PAD.

Although cryoplasty has been proposed as an alternative to conventional angioplasty, a Cochrane review of 7 trials with 478 patients found no evidence of clinically meaningful or consistent benefit. The quality of included studies was low.

A systematic review found no evidence that aspirin or NSAIDs should be discontinued prior to lower limb vascular surgery, although evidence was lacking regarding clopidogrel, abciximab, eptifibatide, and tirofiban.
Gingko biloba has been noted to increase pain-free walking distance compared with placebo.
Homocysteine-lowering therapies for patients with PAD are not recommended by ACC guidelines (2017).

One recent study regarding far-infrared irradiation (FIR), normally used in wound healing, found improved foot skin surface temperature which may be a sign of improved lower extremity circulation and autonomic nervous system regulation.
ACC guidelines (2017) recommend against chelation therapy for treatment of PAD.
Regular exercise improves walking distance and maximal exercise time in patients with intermittent claudication.
A structured, supervised exercise program is recommended by ACC guidelines (2017).
Supervised high-intensity exercise is more effective than unsupervised low-intensity exercise or no exercise with regards to walking ability and distance.

A systematic review of 23 studies found that supervised exercise programs were significantly more effective than unsupervised home-based exercise programs. Adding a level of supervision to home-based programs improved their efficacy.

American College of Cardiology (ACC) and European College of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines both recommend risk factor optimization (smoking cessation, statin therapy, blood pressure management, and glucose control), supervised exercise rehabilitation, and antiplatelet therapy.
Both ACC and ESC guidelines recommend surgical, endovascular, or hybrid revascularization for appropriately selected patients.
While ESC recommends clopidogrel over aspirin to reduce cardiovascular events, ACC guidelines consider them equivalent. In addition, while ACC guidelines recommend cilostazol, ESC guidelines do not.
Patients with infected ischemic ulcers or wet gangrene should be hospitalized for immediate treatment.
Patients with critical limb ischemia should be referred urgently for specialist assessment.
Patients with critical ischemia may present late with tissue loss and ascending infection.
Treating infection, particularly in diabetic patients, is an important part of treatment.
The amputation of digits, forefoot, or even major limbs may be required if parts of the limb are not viable.
Revascularization is the main objective in patients with critical limb ischemia. This can be achieved through endovascular or open surgery, or a combination of both.

Percutaneous transluminal or subintimal angioplasty with or without stenting alone may be sufficient to improve the perfusion to the lower limb. Open surgery may involve endarterectomy or bypass surgery, or a combination of both.
PAD is associated with a significantly increased mortality risk. B
The more severe the PAD, the higher the risk of mortality. B
Patients with intermittent claudication have a relatively low risk of limb loss. B
Patients with critical limb ischemia have a very high mortality rate and high risk of limb loss. B
The more severe the PAD, the higher the risk of mortality.
Coronary artery disease has been reported in up to 80% of PAD patients. Up to 25% of PAD patients have hemodynamically significant carotid artery stenosis.
Patients with critical limb ischemia have a 1-year mortality rate of 20%.

The annual overall cardiovascular event rate in patients with PAD is approximately 6%. Coronary artery disease is the most common cause of death in patients with PAD, accounting for 40% to 60% of deaths, with cerebral artery disease accounting for another 10% to 20% of deaths.

Only 2% to 3.3% of patients with intermittent claudication will require a major amputation. However, in patients with critical limb ischemia, 40% will lose their limb and 20% will lose their life within 6 months.
The primary patency rates of iliac arteries treated with angioplasty are 86%, 82%, and 71% at 1, 3, and 5 years.

The primary patency rate of aortobifemoral bypass grafting carried out for claudication is 85% and 79% at 5 and 10 years, respectively. When carried out for critical limb ischemia, the respective primary patency rates are 80% and 72%.
The primary patency rates after angioplasty of a femoropopliteal stenosis are 77%, 61%, and 55% at 1, 3, and 5 years. When an occlusion is treated, the respective rates are 65%, 48%, and 42%.

The 5-year patency rates for femoropopliteal bypass grafts vary from 39% to 80%, depending on the type of conduit, the outflow vessel, and the indication for treatment (ie, claudication or critical ischemia).
Clinical surveillance is recommended for 2 years after bypass grafts, starting in the immediate postoperative period and carried out at regular intervals (usually every 6 months).
